prize_parts.citation: for their analysis of how electoral rules, constitutions and state capacity shape fiscal policy and economic outcomes

statement.case_for: My ballot and names are unchanged from round 1: a single-part B016 prize to Persson, Tabellini and Besley. After the exchange I still judge it the strongest candidate on the common criteria of originality, scope, maturity and attribution. The Persson-Tabellini programme links electoral rules and constitutional design to fiscal policy and public-goods provision in a formal framework, with empirical work attached. The Besley-Persson programme treats fiscal and legal state capacity as an outcome of political incentives and conflict. The contributions come from long-standing partnerships, so the credit line is more traceable than in a literature credited to eight or more names. The work is about three decades old, has been extended into public finance, macro and development, and later work has often used sharper designs. I have tightened the citation. It now names the specific programmes (electoral rules, constitutions, state capacity), as I said in round 1, and it does not claim causal effects of constitutions from cross-country regressions. I also reordered my alternatives. B014 now comes first because it has a stable trio, a clear separation of theory and policy-rule contributions, and the most explicit support. B042 has the cleanest attribution but no member prefers it, and its collateral channel is weakly identified. These changes concern wording and fallback order, not the preferred configuration.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is empirical credibility. Part of the evidence on constitutional and electoral-rule effects rests on observational cross-country variation and is less secure than the theory. A second reservation is overlap with the 2024 institutions prize. I read that prize as covering colonial-origin institutions and long-run prosperity, but several colleagues read the overlap as more material, and I cannot rule out that the Committee will judge the marginal contribution of a second institutions-related prize to be smaller. Third, B016 is one of the smaller positions, with two explicit supporters (Friberg and me). I do not treat that as evidence about merit in either direction, but it does bear on whether the Committee can converge. The B014 and B032 supporters' criticism that I hold B016 to a lower standard on identification than other candidates is a fair test of my position. Besley's inclusion is also the most contestable part of my proposal, since a Persson-Tabellini pair would be a defensible, tighter alternative.

responses.point: Krusell ranks B014 first with Calvo, Taylor and Woodford. He placed B016 outside his top eight because of partial overlap with the 2024 prize and the contested cross-country identification, and he wants that issue resolved before ranking B016 above the macro candidates.
responses.response: The identification point is mine as much as his, and I do not think the evidence in this exchange resolves it. My answer is that the cross-country regressions are not what the citation should rest on. The formal framework that links political rules to policy outcomes, and the later work using sharper designs, carry the case. I accept that this argument may not meet his threshold, and I accept his comparative judgement under common criteria. Krusell is a frequent co-author of mine, which I disclose and do not adjudicate. I have not counted his support for B014 against it or for it. On B014 itself, I agree maturity is not in doubt, and my remaining concern is attribution across eight names, not merit.

responses.point: Andersson ranks B014 first and argues that the Calvo, Taylor and Woodford trio already covers both theory and applied-policy contributions. He hesitates on B016 because of the 2024 institutions prize and identification problems, and he takes my two-name B007 cut as a sign of diffuse credit there.
responses.response: I accept his point that the trio spans theory (Calvo), contract and rule (Taylor) and the welfare-based policy framework (Woodford), so my theory-versus-policy split question for B014 is largely answered. That is why B014 now leads my alternatives. I would add two clarifications. My B007 ranking was eighth, partly for the diffuse credit he mentions, and the same standard applied to B016 yields a tighter result, because the programmes sit in two long-standing partnerships. Second, on the 2024 prize I still read B016 as concerning how policy is made within existing political systems, not the colonial or long-run origins of institutions. I recognise that this reading is contestable and that he and others weigh the overlap more heavily.

responses.point: Dreber Almenberg ranks B032 first for its transparent quasi-experimental designs and holds observational cross-country evidence to a stricter standard. She regards B016 as field-creating, ranks it third, sees a more material overlap with the 2024 prize, and says she would not oppose a B016 prize on scientific grounds if the identification caveats were reflected in the citation.
responses.response: I take the identification standard seriously and have written the citation to reflect it. It describes the analysis of how rules and capacity shape fiscal outcomes and does not assert specific causal effects. I also accept that B032's local-labour-market evidence is better identified than the B016 cross-country evidence. Where I differ is attribution. Even with Dorn as the third name, B032 leaves Katz out. The task framework also rests on people outside the ballot (Levy, Murnane, Acemoglu, Restrepo). The aggregate magnitude and persistence of the China-shock effects remain debated, as she acknowledges. In my view these considerations roughly offset B032's advantage on identification. I would not dismiss B032 scientifically, and I did not rank it highly in my opening mainly because of that credit structure. I recognise this is a judgement and that she weighs these criteria differently.

responses.point: Friberg ranks B016 first and keeps Besley because he sees state capacity as a distinct achievement and not just an extension of the constitutions work. He regards Besley's inclusion as the most debatable part of his proposal and sees a Persson-Tabellini award as defensible. He reads the 2024 prize as being about long-run colonial and institutional origins, and B016 as about how policy is made inside given political systems.
responses.response: I agree with his reading on both points. I moved to include Besley on his round 1 argument, and I still find it persuasive that omitting the state-capacity strand would make the citation narrower than the contribution. The exchange has not changed that view. I also agree with his emphasis on the formal framework over cross-country regressions, and I used that in drafting the citation. I disclose that I co-authored a paper with him and Tore Ellingsen. Our agreement on B016 should not be read as independent confirmation, since we are the only two members with this preference and share some of the same reasoning. If the Committee prefers a tighter pair, I would accept Persson and Tabellini as a defensible alternative. I am not proposing it, because I think the state-capacity contribution warrants a name.

responses.point: Teorell lists B016 as an alternative and moved to B032 as his preferred part. He keeps B042 as his first alternative, treating Kiyotaki and Moore as the cleanest attribution, but now weights the empirical-anchor concern and the overlap with the 2022 prize more heavily.
responses.response: His revised weighing of B042 matches my own. I keep it among my alternatives for the attribution reasons I gave in round 1, but the evidence behind the collateral channel is mostly theory and calibration, and the 2022 overlap is unresolved. That is why I now put it second after B014. I agree with him that adding Gertler to B042 would bring back the accelerator lineage and the question of Bernanke's earlier recognition, so the two-person core is the right version of that candidate. His disclosed adjacency to the B016 field does not affect my reading of his position. As I said in round 1, I treat the 2024 presentation speech as reflecting no personal preference. I record his move toward B032 as a response to the maturity argument and not as a vote count.

uncertainties: Whether the Committee reads the 2024 institutions prize as leaving enough distinct ground (policy-making within given political systems) for B016, or as making a second institutions-related prize less pressing.

How much weight the partly observational cross-country evidence on constitutional and electoral-rule effects should carry. I rely on the formal framework and later sharper designs, but I have not verified that body of work against sources in this exercise.
Whether Besley should be credited alongside Persson and Tabellini, or whether a two-person award gives cleaner attribution. Alesina, Acemoglu and Robinson also sit outside the cut.

Whether B016, with two explicit supporters, can attract wider agreement, or whether the Committee will converge on B014, B032 or B010. I do not weigh counts as merit and do not seek artificial consensus, but I cannot resolve this from the evidence supplied.

For B014, the unresolved choice between honouring the theoretical originators (Calvo, Taylor, Woodford) and the estimated-model strand (Galí, Gertler, Christiano, Eichenbaum, Smets). Prior-prize facts such as the 2022 and 2024 prizes and Gertler's status are members' stated recollections and are not independently verified here.
statement.conflict_note: The supplied profile documents no co-authorship, institutional tie or other connection to Persson, Tabellini or Besley (B016), to Calvo, Taylor or Woodford (B014), or to Kiyotaki or Moore (B042). In round 1 I noted a possible IIES connection with Persson. The supplied profile does not document it, so I disclose it as possible and unverified. My dynamic political-economy and public-finance work is adjacent to B016. Its documented co-authors (Storesletten, Zilibotti, Rodríguez Mora, Krusell) are not credited on any shortlisted ballot. As chair I wrote the round 1 summary. It counts only explicit statements, and I do not treat it as support for my own position. I am a documented co-author of committee members Krusell and Boppart, who prefer B014, and of Friberg (a 2026 IJIO paper with Tore Ellingsen), who shares my B016 preference. None of them is a credited candidate. I am an IIES colleague of Krusell and Boppart. These connections are disclosed and not adjudicated.
